Those trades carry a 0.5% router fee. Tokens that charge their own transfer tax may not be sellable through the router, so check before you buy.

**What does LP locked mean on an Elysium memecoin?**
It means the coin's trading pool cannot be withdrawn. On ArkhamPad coins, the pool position is held by the launcher contract forever, so neither the creator nor ArkhamPad can pull the liquidity. This rules out a liquidity rug pull. It does not protect the price, which can still fall if holders sell.

**How fast are trades on Elysium?**
Elysium is designed for very fast blocks, with a target of roughly 100 to 200 milliseconds, and high throughput. In practice, trades usually confirm quickly. Deposits from HyperEVM arrive within seconds to a few minutes, while withdrawals through the official bridge back to HyperEVM take about 5.5 days.


# How to Read a Memecoin Chart: Candles, Volume, Market Cap
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/how-to-read-a-memecoin-chart/

A memecoin chart shows how a token's price or market cap moved over time, using candles that record the open, high, low and close for each period. Read it together with volume, buys and sells, and holder data, because a chart alone cannot tell you whether a move came from many traders or a few wallets.

## What does each candle on a memecoin chart show?

A candlestick chart splits time into equal periods. Each candle summarises trading in one period with four values:

- **Open:** the price at the start of the period.
- **Close:** the price at the end of the period.
- **High:** the highest price traded during the period.
- **Low:** the lowest price traded during the period.

The thick part of the candle, called the body, runs from the open to the close. The thin lines above and below, called wicks or shadows, reach the high and the low. On most charts a green candle means the close was above the open, and a red candle means it closed lower.

Wicks carry useful information. A long upper wick means buyers pushed the price up during the period, but sellers pushed it back down before the close. A long lower wick means the opposite: the price dropped, then buyers stepped in. On memecoins, long wicks are common because a single large trade can move the price a lot in a pool with modest liquidity.

## Which timeframe should you use on a memecoin chart?

The timeframe sets how much time each candle covers. ArkhamPad token pages offer 1-minute, 5-minute, 15-minute, 1-hour and 4-hour candles.

- **1m and 5m** show every burst of activity. They are useful in the first hours after a coin launches, when the whole history may be only a few dozen candles long.
- **15m and 1h** smooth out noise and make the overall direction easier to see over a day or two.
- **4h** works best for coins that have traded for several days or longer.

A useful habit is to check two timeframes. A sharp green run on the 1-minute chart may look very different on the 1-hour chart, where it might be a small bounce inside a longer decline. On a new network, most tokens also have short histories. In the first weeks after the [Elysium mainnet launch](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-mainnet-launch/), longer timeframes may show only a handful of candles.

## Should you view the chart in market cap or price?

ArkhamPad charts can show either market cap or price. The shape of the chart is the same in both views, because for a fixed supply, market cap is simply price multiplied by the number of tokens. Only the numbers on the axis change.

Memecoin prices are often tiny. A coin launched on ArkhamPad starts at a market cap of 60 HYPE for a supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens, which works out to a starting price of 0.00000006 HYPE per token. Numbers with that many zeros are hard to read and easy to misjudge.

Market cap is usually easier. Saying a coin went from 60 HYPE to 600 HYPE in market cap is clearer than comparing two prices with seven zeros after the decimal point. It also lets you compare coins with different supplies fairly. The difference is explained in detail in [market cap vs price](https://arkhampad.com/learn/market-cap-vs-price/).

## How do you read volume, buys and sells?

Price shows where a token traded. Volume shows how much traded. A price move on high volume, with many separate trades, says more than the same move on a few trades.

On ArkhamPad, the [Discover page](https://arkhampad.com/) shows each token's 24-hour volume and the number of buys and sells, and every token page has a live trades list. Use them together with the chart:

- **Rising price, rising volume, many buys:** demand is broad. That does not guarantee it continues.
- **Rising price on a few large buys:** one or two wallets may be driving the move, and they can sell just as quickly.
- **Falling price with sells outnumbering buys:** holders are taking profit or leaving.
- **Flat price, very low volume:** interest has faded, and even a small sell may move the price.

If the live trades list shows most volume coming from a few large trades, the chart reflects those traders more than the wider market.

## What do common memecoin chart patterns mean?

Charts do not predict the future, but some shapes appear again and again on new tokens. Recognising them explains what already happened.

- **Launch spike:** a run of tall green candles right after launch, often followed by a sharp pullback as early buyers sell.
- **Long upper wicks near a top:** buyers keep pushing higher, but sellers take the price back each time.
- **Staircase:** a series of higher lows, where each dip is bought at a higher level than the last.
- **Slow bleed:** many small red candles on falling volume. Attention is moving elsewhere.
- **One giant red candle:** a large holder sold into the pool. Check the holders list to see whether other large holders remain.

None of these patterns is a reliable signal on its own. Memecoins can ignore every pattern when news or a single social post shifts attention.

## What can a memecoin chart not tell you?

A chart only shows trades that already happened. It does not show who holds the supply or whether the pool can be drained. Before you buy, also check:

- **Holder concentration.** The top-10 holder share on Discover and the holders list on the token page show how much supply a few wallets control. See [token holders and top-10 concentration](https://arkhampad.com/learn/token-holders-top-10/).
- **Liquidity.** ArkhamPad coins have liquidity locked forever and show an LP locked label. For tokens from elsewhere, find out how the pool is held.
- **Contract and creator.** The token page shows the contract address, creator, pool type, supply and age.

A clean-looking chart on a token where one wallet holds half the supply is far riskier than the chart suggests.

## A simple routine for reading a memecoin chart

1. Open the token from Discover and confirm the contract address.
2. Switch the chart to market cap view so the numbers are easy to compare.
3. Look at the 1-hour or 4-hour chart for the overall direction, then the 1-minute or 5-minute chart for recent action.
4. Check 24-hour volume and buys versus sells.
5. Scan the live trades list for unusually large trades.
6. Check the holders list and the top-10 share.
7. If you trade, size your order so it does not move the price too much, and set slippage with care. See [slippage explained](https://arkhampad.com/learn/slippage-explained/).

If you launched the coin yourself, the same routine shows you how people are trading it. The [memecoin launch checklist](https://arkhampad.com/learn/memecoin-launch-checklist/) covers what to watch in the first 24 hours. Whatever the chart shows, memecoins stay high risk.

## FAQ

**What do green and red candles mean on a crypto chart?**
On most charts, a green candle means the price closed higher than it opened during that period, and a red candle means it closed lower. The body shows the open-to-close range, and the wicks show the highest and lowest prices traded. Colour alone does not tell you how much volume was behind the move.

**What is the best timeframe for trading memecoins?**
There is no single best timeframe. Short timeframes such as 1-minute and 5-minute candles suit brand-new coins with little history. Longer timeframes such as 1-hour and 4-hour candles show the broader trend for coins that have traded for days. Checking one short and one long timeframe gives a more balanced view.

**Why does a memecoin chart have such long wicks?**
Memecoin pools often hold modest liquidity, so one large buy or sell can move the price far within a single candle. If the price then returns before the candle closes, a long wick remains. Frequent long wicks usually mean the price is easy to move, which also means your own trades may have more price impact.

**Is a market cap chart the same as a price chart?**
For a token with a fixed supply, yes in shape. Market cap equals price multiplied by supply, so both lines move by the same percentage. Only the numbers differ. Market cap view is often easier to read for memecoins, whose prices can have many zeros after the decimal point.

**Can a chart show if a memecoin is a rug pull?**
Not on its own. A chart shows past trades, not who holds the supply or whether liquidity can be removed. Check holder concentration, liquidity status, the contract address and the creator as well. On ArkhamPad coins, liquidity is locked forever, so a liquidity rug pull is not possible, though the price can still fall.


# Market Cap vs Price: What Memecoin Traders Should Watch
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/market-cap-vs-price/

Price is what one token costs; market cap is that price multiplied by the token supply, so it shows the value of the whole token. For memecoins, market cap is usually the more useful number, because supplies differ enormously and a low price per token does not mean a coin is cheap.

## What is the difference between market cap and price?

**Price** is what one token costs right now, based on the most recent trade. **Market cap** (market capitalisation) is the price multiplied by the number of tokens in supply. It is the value the market is currently placing on the whole token.

Market cap = price × supply

Say a coin has a supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens and the last trade was at 0.000001 HYPE per token. Its market cap is 1,000 HYPE. If the price doubles to 0.000002 HYPE, the market cap doubles to 2,000 HYPE. Price and market cap move by the same percentage, as long as the supply does not change.

Price describes one token. Market cap describes the whole coin.

## Why a low token price does not mean a coin is cheap

Many new traders look for coins with a very low price, expecting that a token worth a tiny fraction of a cent has more room to grow. This is called unit bias, and it is one of the most common mistakes in memecoin trading.

Price alone tells you nothing about value, because supplies vary enormously. Consider two hypothetical coins:

- Coin A has 1,000,000 tokens at 1 HYPE each. Market cap: 1,000,000 HYPE.
- Coin B has 1,000,000,000,000 tokens at 0.000001 HYPE each. Market cap: 1,000,000 HYPE.

Coin B's price looks a million times cheaper, yet both coins are valued the same. For either one to double, the market has to add another 1,000,000 HYPE of value. The low price of Coin B gives it no advantage.

When you compare coins, compare market caps. Ask how large a market cap the coin would need to reach for the return you have in mind, and whether that is realistic for a memecoin.

## Circulating supply, total supply and fully diluted value

Not every token has its whole supply in the market. Many crypto projects reserve tokens for a team, investors or future releases. That is why you will see several related terms:

- **Total supply:** every token that exists.
- **Circulating supply:** tokens that are actually in the market and can be traded.
- **Fully diluted value (FDV):** price multiplied by total supply, including tokens not yet circulating.

When a large share of supply is reserved, market cap based on circulating supply can look small while FDV is much larger. When those reserved tokens are released later, they can add heavy selling pressure.

Coins launched on ArkhamPad avoid this gap. The total supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens goes into the pool at launch, with no team allocation and no presale. Circulating supply and total supply are the same from the start, so market cap and FDV match. For tokens launched elsewhere, check the supply details and the holders list before relying on any market cap figure.

## How does buying change a memecoin's market cap?

On Elysium, memecoins trade in automated pools rather than on an order book. When you buy, you add HYPE to the pool and take tokens out. Fewer tokens remain in the pool, so the pool's price rises. Selling does the reverse.

A coin launched on ArkhamPad starts at a market cap of 60 HYPE. Every buy moves that number up and every sell moves it down. Because the pool is small early on, even modest buys can move the market cap a long way. That is why young memecoins can multiply in value within minutes, and fall just as fast.

This also explains price impact: the bigger your trade compared with the pool, the further it moves the price against you. A large order in a thin pool gets a worse average price than a small one.

## Is market cap the money you could actually cash out?

No. Market cap is the last trade price multiplied by the supply. It assumes every token could be sold at that price, which is never true.

If holders tried to sell a large share of the supply, each sale would push the price lower, and the HYPE they received would be far less than the market cap suggested. How much HYPE can actually come out depends on the liquidity in the pool and how much is sold.

Say a hypothetical coin shows a market cap of 10,000 HYPE. That does not mean 10,000 HYPE is sitting in the pool waiting to be withdrawn. Selling even a modest fraction of the supply could drop the price sharply. Treat market cap as a measure of how the market values a coin at this moment, not as money that exists.

## How do you use market cap when trading Elysium memecoins?

ArkhamPad's [Discover page](https://arkhampad.com/) shows market cap, 24-hour change, volume, buys and sells, and holders for every HYPE-paired token on Elysium. To trade, you can [log in with just an email](https://arkhampad.com/learn/trade-crypto-with-email-login/).

A few practical habits:

- **Use the launch as a reference point.** ArkhamPad coins all start at 60 HYPE. A coin at 600 HYPE has grown about 10 times since launch.
- **Read charts in market cap view.** Token pages let you switch the chart between market cap and price. See [how to read a memecoin chart](https://arkhampad.com/learn/how-to-read-a-memecoin-chart/).
- **Remember the price of HYPE.** These coins trade against HYPE, the same asset used on HyperEVM and bridged 1:1 to Elysium (see [Elysium vs HyperEVM](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-vs-hyperevm/)). A coin's value in dollars moves with both its own HYPE price and the price of HYPE itself.
- **Compare like with like.** Compare coins by market cap, never by price per token.

For a broader overview of the tokens on the network, see the [Elysium memecoins guide](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-memecoins-guide/).

## Why can volume matter more than market cap?

Market cap tells you how a coin is valued. Volume tells you how actively it trades. A coin with a high market cap and almost no volume can be hard to sell without moving the price. A coin with steady volume relative to its size usually has more active interest.

Volume also drives creator earnings. On ArkhamPad coins, every trade pays a 1% pool fee, and 30% of those fees go to the coin's creator. Creator income depends on how much the coin trades, not on its market cap. See [creator fees](https://arkhampad.com/learn/earn-creator-fees/) for how this works.

Neither number makes a memecoin safe. Market caps on new coins can fall to a fraction of their peak within hours. Only trade amounts you can afford to lose.

## FAQ

**Is it better to buy a coin with a low price?**
No. A low price per token says nothing about value, because the supply can be huge. A coin priced at a tiny fraction of a cent can have the same market cap as a coin priced at 1 HYPE. Compare market caps instead, and ask how much value the market would need to add for the coin to reach your target.

**How do you calculate market cap in crypto?**
Multiply the current price per token by the supply. A coin with 1,000,000,000 tokens trading at 0.000001 HYPE has a market cap of 1,000 HYPE. Some sites use circulating supply and show fully diluted value separately using total supply. For ArkhamPad coins the two match, because the whole supply goes into the pool at launch.

**What is the starting market cap of an ArkhamPad coin?**
Every coin created on ArkhamPad starts at a market cap of 60 HYPE for its full supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens. That equals a starting price of 0.00000006 HYPE per token. Because every coin starts from the same point, you can quickly see how much a coin has grown since launch by comparing its current market cap with 60 HYPE.

**Can a memecoin's market cap go to zero?**
In practice it can get very close. If buyers disappear and holders keep selling, the price falls toward zero and so does the market cap. Locked liquidity, as on ArkhamPad coins, means the pool cannot be withdrawn, but it does not hold the price up. Many memecoins lose most of their value, so trade with that in mind.

**What is the difference between market cap and liquidity?**
Market cap is the last price multiplied by the supply. Liquidity is the amount of assets actually available in the pool to trade against. A coin can show a large market cap while its pool holds far less, so selling a big position can push the price well below what the market cap implies.


# Slippage Explained: What to Set and Why Trades Fail
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/slippage-explained/

Slippage is the difference between the result you are quoted and the result your trade actually gets, caused mainly by other trades landing before yours. Your slippage setting is the most you will accept; if the price moves further, the trade fails instead of filling at a worse price. On ArkhamPad you can choose 1%, 3%, 5% (the default) or 10%.

## What is slippage in crypto?

When you swap tokens in a pool, you see a quote first: how many tokens you should receive for the HYPE you pay, or how much HYPE you should receive for the tokens you sell. That quote is based on the state of the pool at the moment you looked.

By the time your transaction is processed, the pool may have changed. Other traders may have bought or sold in between. **Slippage** is the difference between the quoted result and the result you actually get.

Slippage can work in either direction. If other traders sold just before your buy, you may receive slightly more tokens than quoted. On busy memecoins, though, it usually works against you, because many people buy into the same moves at the same time.

## What is the difference between slippage and price impact?

The two are related but not the same.

- **Price impact** is how much your own trade moves the price. In a pool, buying takes tokens out and pushes the price up as your order fills. The larger your trade compared with the liquidity in the pool, the bigger the impact. The quote you see already includes it.
- **Slippage** is any further change between the quote and execution, mostly caused by other trades landing first.

Price impact matters a lot on new memecoins. A coin launched on ArkhamPad starts at a market cap of 60 HYPE, so early on the pool is small and even a modest buy can move the price noticeably. Check the quote before you confirm. If it gives you far fewer tokens than you expected, your order is large for that pool. How price relates to pool size is covered in [market cap vs price](https://arkhampad.com/learn/market-cap-vs-price/).

## How does minimum received protect you?

Your slippage setting turns into a hard limit called **minimum received**. It is the least you will accept from the trade. If the trade would deliver less, it does not go through.

Say you want to buy a coin and the quote shows 1,000,000 tokens. With slippage set to 5%, the minimum received is 950,000 tokens. If the price moves so that your HYPE would buy only 940,000 tokens when the trade executes, the transaction is rejected and your HYPE stays in your wallet. If it would buy 980,000, the trade goes through and you receive 980,000.

The same applies to sells. If you sell tokens with a quote of 10 HYPE and 3% slippage, the minimum received is 9.7 HYPE.

On ArkhamPad, the quote and the minimum received are shown before you trade, so you can see exactly what your setting allows.

## What slippage should you set?

ArkhamPad offers four settings: 1%, 3%, 5% and 10%. The default is 5%. There is no single right answer, but a simple guide helps:

- **1%:** for calm tokens and small orders. Lowest risk of a poor fill, but trades fail more often when the price is moving.
- **3%:** a reasonable choice for tokens that trade steadily without big swings.
- **5% (default):** a balance for typical memecoin trading, where prices move quickly.
- **10%:** for very fast markets, such as the first minutes after a launch, when lower settings keep failing. You accept that you may get a noticeably worse price.

A higher setting does not make your trade more expensive by itself. It only raises how much worse than the quote you are willing to accept. On a fast-moving coin, though, a wide setting means you may actually receive that worse result. Start lower and only raise it when you understand why trades are failing.

## Why do crypto trades fail?

A failed trade is frustrating, but it usually has a clear cause. The most common ones:

1. **Slippage exceeded.** The price moved more than your setting allowed, so the minimum received could not be met. This is the protection working as intended. Get a fresh quote and try again, or raise slippage one step.
2. **Not enough HYPE for gas.** Network fees on Elysium are paid in HYPE from your balance. If you spend your entire balance on a buy, there may be nothing left for the fee. Keep a little HYPE aside. See [Elysium gas fees](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-gas-fees/).
3. **Token transfer tax.** Some tokens charge their own tax whenever they are transferred. These may not be sellable through the ArkhamPad router.
4. **Insufficient balance.** The amount entered is more than your wallet holds, often because a previous trade or fee already used part of it.

On EVM networks, a transaction that fails after reaching the chain can still use some gas. On Elysium that cost is very low, but repeated failures still add up.

## How do you reduce slippage on memecoins?

- **Trade smaller amounts.** A smaller order has less price impact and is less likely to fail. You can split a large buy into a few smaller ones, keeping in mind that each trade pays its own fees.
- **Avoid the busiest moments.** The first minutes after a launch, or right after a coin is shared widely, are when prices move fastest.
- **Refresh the quote.** If you waited a while before confirming, get a new quote so the minimum received reflects the current price.
- **Check the pool before a big trade.** If what you receive drops sharply as you increase the amount, the pool is thin for that size.
- **Have funds ready.** Bridge HYPE in advance on the [Bridge page](https://arkhampad.com/bridge/) so you are not rushing. The guides to [bridging HYPE to Elysium](https://arkhampad.com/learn/bridge-hype-to-elysium/) and [buying with USDC](https://arkhampad.com/learn/buy-elysium-tokens-with-usdc/) cover both ways in.

For the full buy and sell flow, see [how to buy and sell Elysium tokens](https://arkhampad.com/learn/how-to-buy-elysium-tokens/).

## Does Elysium's design affect slippage?

Partly. Elysium is designed for very fast blocks, with a target of about 100 to 200 milliseconds. A shorter gap between your quote and the block that includes your trade gives the price less time to drift.

At launch, a single sequencer orders transactions by priority fee, and there is no public mempool where pending trades sit in view of everyone. Even so, other trades can still land before yours, especially on popular coins. Your slippage setting and minimum received remain your real protection.

No setting protects you from the price falling after your trade completes. Memecoins are highly volatile, so only trade amounts you can afford to lose.

## FAQ

**What is a good slippage setting for memecoins?**
On ArkhamPad the default is 5%, which suits most memecoin trades. Use 1% or 3% for calmer tokens and small orders. Use 10% only in very fast markets, such as right after a launch, when lower settings keep failing. Remember that a higher setting means you accept a possibly worse price in exchange for a better chance the trade fills.

**Why did my trade fail with a slippage error?**
The price moved more than your slippage setting allowed between the quote and execution, so the trade could not deliver your minimum received and was rejected. Your funds stay in your wallet. Refresh the quote and try again, trade a smaller amount, or raise slippage one step if you accept a possibly worse price.

**Does high slippage mean I pay more?**
Not automatically. Slippage tolerance is a limit, not a fee. With 10% slippage you may still receive close to the quote if the price barely moves. But you allow the trade to fill up to 10% worse, and on fast-moving coins that can happen. Fees, such as the 1% pool fee on ArkhamPad coins, are separate from slippage.

**What is minimum received in crypto?**
Minimum received is the smallest amount your trade will accept, calculated from the quote and your slippage setting. For example, a quote of 1,000,000 tokens with 5% slippage gives a minimum of 950,000 tokens. If the trade would deliver less, it fails instead of filling. ArkhamPad shows the minimum received before you confirm.

**Why can't I sell a token through the router?**
Some tokens charge their own tax whenever they are transferred. The amount that arrives is then less than a normal swap expects, so these tokens may not be sellable through the ArkhamPad router. Check whether a token has a transfer tax before you buy, because being unable to sell easily is a serious risk.


# Top 10 Holders in Crypto: What Concentration Tells You
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/token-holders-top-10/

Top-10 holder concentration is the share of a token's supply held by its ten largest wallets. A high share means a few wallets can push the price down sharply by selling, so it is one of the first things to check before buying a memecoin. On ArkhamPad, Discover shows each token's top-10 share and every token page lists holders with their percentage of supply.

## What does top-10 holder concentration mean?

Every token balance sits in a wallet address, and anyone can see which addresses hold how much. **Holder concentration** describes how that supply is spread out. The most common way to measure it is the **top-10 holder share**: the percentage of total supply held by the ten largest addresses combined.

Say a coin has a supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens and its ten largest wallets hold 400,000,000 between them. Its top-10 share is 40%. The other 60% is spread across every remaining holder.

It is a simple number, but it answers an important question: how few people would need to sell to move the price a lot?

## Why do top 10 holders matter for memecoins?

Memecoins trade in pools. When a holder sells, they put tokens into the pool and take HYPE out, which pushes the price down. The bigger the sale compared with the pool, the bigger the drop.

If supply is spread across many small holders, no single seller can do much damage. If a few wallets hold a large share, any one of them can cause a sharp fall by selling, and others often follow when they see it happen. Large holders are often called whales.

High concentration also makes charts less trustworthy. A steady climb may simply reflect one or two wallets buying, and those wallets can reverse at any time. That is why holder data should be read alongside the chart, as covered in [how to read a memecoin chart](https://arkhampad.com/learn/how-to-read-a-memecoin-chart/).

## Which addresses in a holder list are not real holders?

Not every large address is a person who can sell. Before you judge a top-10 share, look at who the largest addresses are.

- **The liquidity pool.** The pool contract holds the tokens available to trade, and it often appears as the largest holder. Those tokens are not held by a trader; they are what buyers purchase from.
- **Burn addresses.** Tokens sent to an address nobody controls are effectively destroyed.
- **Other contracts.** Some addresses belong to smart contracts rather than individuals.

This matters most for brand-new coins. On ArkhamPad, the whole supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens goes into the pool at launch, so at first almost everything sits in the pool. As people buy, tokens move from the pool into wallets. A very high top-10 share on a coin that is minutes old may simply mean the pool still holds most of the supply. Check whether the largest holder is the pool before drawing conclusions.

## What top-10 holder percentage is safe?

There is no universal safe number. What counts as risky depends on the token's age, how much of the supply is still in the pool and who the large wallets belong to. A few guidelines help:

- **Look at individual wallets, not only the total.** Ten wallets holding 3% each is very different from one wallet holding 25% and nine holding 0.5% each.
- **Set aside the pool and burn addresses** when you think about how much supply traders control.
- **Check the creator.** The token page shows the creator's address. If the creator's wallet is among the largest holders, they can sell into anyone who buys after them. On ArkhamPad, a creator can make an optional first buy at launch, and those tokens appear in the holders list like any other.
- **Watch for linked wallets.** Several mid-sized wallets that all bought at the same moment may belong to the same person.
- **Watch the trend.** Concentration falling over time as more people buy is generally healthier than concentration rising.

Low concentration does not make a coin safe. It only reduces one specific risk.

## How do you check token holders on ArkhamPad?

1. Open [Discover](https://arkhampad.com/). Every HYPE-paired token on Elysium is listed with its holder count and top-10 holder share.
2. Use the top-10 share to decide which coins deserve a closer look.
3. Open the token page and go to the holders list. Each address is shown with its percentage of supply.
4. Note the creator address shown on the token page and look for it in the list.
5. Watch the live trades list for unusually large sells.
6. Check again later. Concentration changes as people buy and sell.

## Does a high holder count mean a coin is safe?

Not by itself. Holder count only tells you how many addresses hold at least some of the token. It says nothing about how the supply is divided.

A coin can have thousands of holders and still have most of its supply in five wallets. Holder counts can also be inflated by sending tiny amounts to many new addresses. Read holder count and top-10 share together. A growing number of holders with a falling top-10 share is a better sign than either number alone.

## How does holder concentration relate to rug pulls?

A classic rug pull happens when a creator removes the pool's liquidity, leaving holders unable to sell. On ArkhamPad coins this is not possible, because the pool position is held by the launcher contract forever and nobody can withdraw it. [Locked liquidity explained](https://arkhampad.com/learn/locked-liquidity-explained/) covers how this works.

Concentration creates a different risk, sometimes called a dump or soft rug: a large holder sells a big position into the pool. Locked liquidity means there is always a pool to sell into, but it does not stop the price falling when a whale sells. That is why top-10 share is worth checking even on coins with locked liquidity. Other warning signs are listed in [how to spot a rug pull](https://arkhampad.com/learn/spot-a-rug-pull/).

When a large sell hits, prices can drop within seconds. If you are selling at the same time, a tight [slippage setting](https://arkhampad.com/learn/slippage-explained/) may cause your trade to fail, while a wide one may fill at a much lower price. Selling into the pool is quick, but moving HYPE back to HyperEVM through the official bridge takes about 5.5 days, as explained in [Elysium withdrawal time](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-withdrawal-time/). Memecoins are high risk, so size positions with that in mind.

## FAQ

**What does top 10 holders mean in crypto?**
It is the share of a token's total supply held by its ten largest wallet addresses combined. If the ten biggest wallets hold 400 million tokens of a 1 billion supply, the top-10 share is 40%. A high share means a small group can move the price sharply by selling, so traders use it as a quick concentration check.

**Is it bad if one wallet holds a lot of a token?**
It depends whose wallet it is. If it is the liquidity pool or a burn address, those tokens are not held by a trader. If it is the creator or another individual, that wallet can sell a large amount at once and push the price down sharply. Check the address before you judge the number.

**Why does a new ArkhamPad coin show such high concentration?**
At launch, the entire supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens goes into the pool, so the pool holds nearly everything. As people buy, tokens move from the pool into their wallets and the supply spreads out. Early on, a high top-10 share often reflects the pool rather than a few traders, so check the largest address first.

**Where can I see token holders on Elysium?**
On ArkhamPad, the Discover page shows the holder count and top-10 holder share for every HYPE-paired token on Elysium. Each token page has a holders list with every address and its percentage of supply, alongside the contract address, creator, pool type, supply and age of the token.

**Can whales dump a token with locked liquidity?**
Yes. Locked liquidity only means the pool itself cannot be withdrawn. Any holder, including a large one, can still sell tokens into the pool. A big sale pushes the price down, sometimes sharply. Locked liquidity prevents a liquidity rug pull, but it does not protect the price from falling.


# How to Create a Token on Elysium in 30 Seconds
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/create-a-token-on-elysium/

You can create a token on Elysium with ArkhamPad in about 30 seconds: enter a name, ticker and image, optionally add a description, links and a first buy, then confirm one transaction. Every coin has 1,000,000,000 tokens, all placed in a locked Uniswap v3 style pool against HYPE at a starting market cap of 60 HYPE, and the creator earns 30% of trading fees.

## What does it mean to create a token on Elysium?

Creating a token means deploying a new smart contract that defines a coin, and then giving it a market so people can buy and sell it. On Elysium, a Layer 2 for the Hyperliquid ecosystem built by Kinetiq, this works like on any EVM chain, because Elysium runs standard Arbitrum Nitro. If you are new to the chain, start with [what Elysium is](https://arkhampad.com/learn/what-is-elysium/).

Doing this by hand takes code, testing and a separate step to add liquidity. A launchpad bundles all of it into one form and one transaction. On ArkhamPad you do not write code, choose a supply or set up a pool yourself. The launcher contract does that for you, the same way for every coin.

## What you need before you start

The list is short:

- **An account.** Log in with email, Google or an existing wallet. Email and Google users get an embedded wallet created automatically, with no seed phrase to write down to get started. See [trading with just an email](https://arkhampad.com/learn/trade-crypto-with-email-login/).
- **A little HYPE.** Elysium uses HYPE for gas, so you need some in your balance to pay the network fee. If you plan a first buy, you need HYPE for that too. You can add HYPE or USDC on the [Bridge page](https://arkhampad.com/bridge/), or follow the guide to [bridge HYPE to Elysium](https://arkhampad.com/learn/bridge-hype-to-elysium/).
- **A name, a ticker and an image.** Pick these before you open the form. They cannot be an afterthought, because they are what people see first on Discover.

Optional: a short description and links (website, X, Telegram). Coins with a clear story and working links are easier for buyers to trust.

## How to create a token on ArkhamPad, step by step

1. Open [Create](https://arkhampad.com/create/) and log in.
2. Enter the coin name and ticker. Keep the ticker short and easy to type.
3. Upload the image. A square image reads best in lists and on the token page.
4. Add a description and links if you have them.
5. Decide whether to make a first buy, and how much HYPE to spend on it.
6. Review and confirm. The coin is deployed, the pool is created and your first buy, if any, happens in the same transaction.

The whole process takes about 30 seconds. When it finishes, your coin has its own token page with a chart, a buy and sell box, live trades and a holders list, and it appears on Discover with the rest of the Elysium market.

## What happens at launch: supply, pool and starting market cap

Every ArkhamPad coin follows the same rules, which makes them easy to compare:

- **Total supply:** 1,000,000,000 tokens.
- **Distribution:** the entire supply goes into the pool at launch. There is no team allocation and no presale.
- **Pool:** a Uniswap v3 style concentrated-liquidity pool paired against wrapped HYPE, with a 1% fee on every trade.
- **Starting market cap:** 60 HYPE for the whole supply.
- **Liquidity:** locked forever inside the launcher contract.

Because nobody receives tokens for free, everyone, including the creator, gets tokens the same way: by buying from the pool. The price then moves with demand. Buys push it up and sells push it down.

## Should you make a first buy?

The first buy is optional. It lets the creator buy tokens in the same transaction that creates the coin, before anyone else can trade. Some creators like it because it shows they have something at stake. Others skip it so they hold nothing and the chart starts clean.

Things to weigh:

- A large first buy gives you a big share of supply. Traders check [top-10 holder concentration](https://arkhampad.com/learn/token-holders-top-10/), and a creator holding a large share can make buyers cautious.
- Only spend what you can afford to lose. Memecoins are risky, and most new coins never get much trading.
- If you sell your first buy later, everyone can see it in the live trades list.

## How creators earn from their coin

Every trade pays the 1% pool fee. ArkhamPad sends 30% of those trading fees to the coin's creator and keeps 70%. Fees are collected from the pool and paid out in HYPE and in the coin. In other words, the creator earns about 0.3% of the coin's trading volume.

The full breakdown has worked examples. The short version: fees depend on volume, not on price, so a coin that keeps trading keeps paying its creator.

## Why locked liquidity makes launches safer

On many chains, the person who adds liquidity can later pull it out and leave holders with a coin nobody can sell. On ArkhamPad that is not possible. The pool position is held by the launcher contract and cannot be withdrawn by anyone, not the creator and not ArkhamPad. These coins show an "LP locked" label on Discover. Read more in [locked liquidity explained](https://arkhampad.com/learn/locked-liquidity-explained/).

Locked liquidity removes one type of scam. It does not guarantee a price. Holders can still sell, and the price can still fall a long way.

## After you launch

Launching is the easy part. Getting people to notice the coin is the real work. Share the token page to X from the token page itself, post the contract address so people do not buy copies, and be present where your community talks. For a plan covering the first day, use the [memecoin launch checklist](https://arkhampad.com/learn/memecoin-launch-checklist/).

## FAQ

**How long does it take to create a token on Elysium?**
On ArkhamPad it takes about 30 seconds. You fill in a name, ticker and image, add optional details and an optional first buy, and confirm one transaction. The contract, the pool and your first buy are created together, and the coin appears on Discover with its own token page.

**Do I need to know how to code to launch a token?**
No. ArkhamPad handles the token contract, the supply and the pool for you. You only provide the name, ticker, image and optional description and links. Because Elysium is a full EVM chain, developers can also deploy their own contracts with normal tools, but that is not needed to launch a coin.

**What does it cost to create a token on ArkhamPad?**
You pay the Elysium network fee in HYPE, which is very low, plus whatever you choose to spend on an optional first buy. Keep a little HYPE in your balance so the transaction can go through. You can add HYPE or USDC on the Bridge page.

**How many tokens does a new coin have?**
Every ArkhamPad coin has a total supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens. All of it goes into the pool at launch, with no team allocation and no presale. The starting market cap is 60 HYPE for the whole supply, and the price moves as people buy and sell.

**Can I change my coin's name or ticker after launch?**
Plan as if you cannot. The name and ticker are part of the token itself and are what traders search for on Discover and see in their wallets. Check spelling and the image before you confirm, because launching a second coin to fix a typo splits attention and confuses buyers.


# Creator Fees: Earn 30% of Trading Fees on Your Coin
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/earn-creator-fees/

On ArkhamPad, every trade of a coin pays a 1% pool fee, and 30% of those fees go to the coin's creator. That works out to about 0.3% of trading volume: for example, $100,000 of volume creates $1,000 in pool fees, of which $300 goes to the creator. Fees are paid out in HYPE and in the coin.

## What are memecoin creator fees?

Creator fees are a share of trading fees paid to the person who launched a coin. They reward creators for building activity around their coin instead of for selling their own tokens. On ArkhamPad, the creator is whoever launched the coin from the [Create](https://arkhampad.com/create/) page, and the share is fixed for every coin: 30% of trading fees.

This matters because it changes incentives. Without fees, the only way a creator makes money is by buying early and selling later, which pushes the price down for everyone else. With fees, a creator can earn from steady trading while holding nothing at all.

## Where the fee comes from: the 1% pool fee

Every ArkhamPad coin trades in a Uniswap v3 style concentrated-liquidity pool against wrapped HYPE. That pool charges a 1% fee on every trade, buys and sells alike. The fee is taken from the trade itself, so the trader pays it as part of the swap.

The fees are then split:

- **30%** to the coin's creator.
- **70%** to ArkhamPad.

So the creator's share equals 30% of 1%, which is **0.3% of trading volume**. This is separate from the Elysium network fee, which is paid in HYPE to the chain and is not shared with anyone on the launchpad. See [Elysium gas fees](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-gas-fees/) for how network costs work.

## How much can a creator earn? Worked examples

The examples below are hypothetical. They show the math, not what any coin will do. Most coins see little volume.

- **$10,000 of volume:** pool fees are $100. The creator's 30% is **$30**.
- **$100,000 of volume:** pool fees are $1,000. The creator's 30% is **$300**.
- **$1,000,000 of volume:** pool fees are $10,000. The creator's 30% is **$3,000**.

The same math works in HYPE. If a coin trades 1,000 HYPE of volume, the pool collects 10 HYPE in fees and the creator's share is 3 HYPE.

A quick rule: multiply volume by 0.003 to estimate the creator's share. Volume counts both buys and sells. A trader who buys 50 HYPE worth and later sells 50 HYPE worth adds 100 HYPE of volume, which pays 1 HYPE in pool fees and 0.3 HYPE to the creator.

## Why creator fees follow volume, not price

A common mistake is to think a higher market cap means higher fees. It does not, at least not directly. Fees are a percentage of what is traded, so a coin that stays at a modest market cap but trades actively can pay its creator more than a coin that spikes once and goes quiet.

If you want to understand the difference between those numbers, read [market cap vs price](https://arkhampad.com/learn/market-cap-vs-price/). For creators, the takeaway is simple: activity over time is what pays. One busy hour after launch is worth less than a coin people keep trading for weeks.

## Are creator fees paid in HYPE or in the coin?

Both. Fees are collected from the pool and paid out in HYPE and in the coin. In a Uniswap v3 style pool, the fee is charged in the token the trader puts in. That generally means fees on buys accrue in HYPE, and fees on sells accrue in the coin.

What this means for you:

- The HYPE part is a fixed amount of HYPE. Its dollar value moves with the HYPE price.
- The coin part is worth whatever your coin is worth. If you sell those tokens, that sale goes through the pool like any other trade and affects the price.
- Some creators keep the coin portion to show commitment. That choice is yours, and buyers can see creator wallet activity on the token page.

## Moving your earnings

Creator fees are paid on Elysium, so you can use the HYPE to trade other coins right away. Keep a little HYPE for gas, since every transaction on Elysium pays its network fee in HYPE. To learn what else HYPE does on the chain, see [HYPE on Elysium](https://arkhampad.com/learn/hype-on-elysium/).

If you want to move HYPE back to HyperEVM, the official bridge takes about 5.5 days because withdrawals finalize after a challenge period. The reasons are explained in [Elysium withdrawal time](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-withdrawal-time/). A faster exit route is being worked on, but there is no date yet.

## How to grow fees without hurting holders

Fees reward creators who keep their coin alive. Practical habits that help:

- Keep links and the description accurate, and post the contract address so buyers do not get copies.
- Share updates, not price promises. Promising returns damages trust and can cause legal problems.
- Avoid holding a huge share of supply. A concentrated holder list scares traders away.
- Be visible. Coins with an active creator tend to keep conversations, and trading, going.

Fees are never guaranteed. A coin with no trading pays nothing. To get started, see [how to create a token on Elysium](https://arkhampad.com/learn/create-a-token-on-elysium/).

## FAQ

**How much do memecoin creators earn on ArkhamPad?**
Creators get 30% of the 1% pool fee, which equals about 0.3% of their coin's trading volume. As a hypothetical example, $100,000 of volume produces $1,000 in pool fees and $300 for the creator. Earnings depend entirely on how much the coin trades, and many coins trade very little.

**Do creators earn fees when people sell?**
Yes. The 1% pool fee applies to every trade, buys and sells. Both count toward volume, and the creator receives 30% of the fees from each. In a Uniswap v3 style pool the fee is charged in the token being sold into the pool, so sell fees generally accrue in the coin.

**Do I need to hold my own coin to earn creator fees?**
No. Creator fees come from trading volume, not from the creator's holdings. You can launch without a first buy and still earn 30% of trading fees. Holding some tokens is a personal choice, and buyers often look at how much the creator holds before deciding.

**Who gets the other 70% of trading fees?**
The other 70% of the pool fees goes to ArkhamPad. The split is the same for every coin launched on ArkhamPad. The Elysium network fee, paid in HYPE for each transaction, is separate and goes to the chain, not to the creator or ArkhamPad.

**Is the 0.5% router fee shared with creators?**
No. The 0.5% router fee applies only when you trade tokens launched elsewhere through the ArkhamPad router. ArkhamPad coins pay no router fee at all. Creator fees come only from the 1% pool fee charged on trades of ArkhamPad coins, and the creator receives 30% of that pool fee.


# Locked Liquidity Explained: Why It Matters
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/locked-liquidity-explained/

Locked liquidity means the tokens and HYPE in a coin's trading pool cannot be withdrawn by the person who added them. It prevents a liquidity rug pull, where the creator removes the pool and leaves holders unable to sell. On ArkhamPad, every coin's pool position is held by the launcher contract forever and cannot be withdrawn by anyone, not the creator and not ArkhamPad.

## What is liquidity in crypto?

Liquidity is how easily you can buy or sell something without moving its price much. For a new token, liquidity usually lives in a liquidity pool: a smart contract that holds two assets, such as a memecoin and wrapped HYPE, and trades them against each other using a formula. When you buy, you put HYPE in and take tokens out. When you sell, you do the reverse.

The pool is what makes trading possible at all. No pool, no market. A deeper pool also means smaller price moves per trade, which is why [slippage](https://arkhampad.com/learn/slippage-explained/) is lower on coins with more liquidity.

## What is an LP position?

Whoever adds assets to a pool receives an LP position, short for liquidity provider position. In Uniswap v3 style pools this is usually an NFT that records how much was deposited and in which price range. The holder of that position can normally withdraw the assets at any time and collect the fees the position has earned.

That control is the key point. If one wallet owns the entire LP position of a new coin, that wallet effectively owns the market for that coin.

## How a liquidity rug pull works

A liquidity rug pull is the classic memecoin scam:

1. Someone launches a token and adds it to a pool with some HYPE.
2. Buyers arrive and add more HYPE to the pool by buying.
3. The creator withdraws the LP position, taking out the HYPE and the tokens.
4. The pool is now empty or nearly empty. Holders still have tokens, but there is nothing to sell them into.

It can happen in seconds and cannot be undone. This is why experienced traders check liquidity before anything else. For the full list of warning signs, see [how to spot a rug pull](https://arkhampad.com/learn/spot-a-rug-pull/).

## What does LP locked mean?

"LP locked" means the LP position cannot be withdrawn by its creator, either for a set time or permanently. There are a few common ways this is done:

- **Time lock:** the position goes into a locking contract that releases it after a date. Safe until that date, then not.
- **Burned:** the position is sent to an address nobody controls. Permanent, but the fees it earns are usually lost too.
- **Held by a contract:** the position stays inside a contract that has no function to withdraw it, while still collecting trading fees.

The details matter. A lock that ends next week is very different from a permanent one, so always check which kind you are looking at.

## How ArkhamPad locks liquidity

Every coin created on ArkhamPad uses the third approach. When a coin launches, its entire 1,000,000,000 token supply goes into a Uniswap v3 style pool against wrapped HYPE. The pool position is held by the launcher contract and cannot be withdrawn by anyone, not the creator and not ArkhamPad. There is no unlock date.

The position still collects the 1% pool fee on every trade. Those fees are collected from the pool and split 30% to the creator and 70% to ArkhamPad, paid in HYPE and in the coin. So the creator has a reason to keep the coin active, but no way to remove the market.

On Discover, ArkhamPad coins show an **LP locked** label, so you can tell them apart from tokens launched elsewhere at a glance.

## What locked liquidity does not protect you from

Locked liquidity removes one specific risk. It is not a safety guarantee. Other ways to lose money remain:

- **Holders selling.** Anyone who bought can sell. If large holders sell, the price drops, even though the pool is still there. Check [top-10 holder concentration](https://arkhampad.com/learn/token-holders-top-10/) before buying.
- **Demand fading.** Most memecoins lose interest quickly. A locked pool still lets you sell, but maybe at a much lower price.
- **Copycats.** Someone can launch a coin with the same name. Always check the contract address.
- **Tokens from elsewhere.** On Discover you can see every HYPE-paired token on Elysium, from every launchpad. Only ArkhamPad coins carry the LP locked label. Other tokens may have different rules, and some charge transfer taxes that stop them from being sold through the router.

Memecoins are high risk. Only use money you can afford to lose. For a wider overview, read the [Elysium memecoins guide](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-memecoins-guide/).

## How to check liquidity before you buy

A quick routine before every buy:

1. Look for the LP locked label on Discover, or check the pool type on the token page.
2. Look at the holders list and the share held by the top 10 wallets.
3. Read the live trades list. A steady mix of buyers and sellers is healthier than a few big wallets.
4. Check the quote before you confirm. If a small buy moves the price a lot, liquidity is thin.

When you are ready, the steps to trade are in [how to buy Elysium tokens](https://arkhampad.com/learn/how-to-buy-elysium-tokens/).

## FAQ

**What is locked liquidity in simple terms?**
Locked liquidity means the money and tokens in a coin's trading pool cannot be taken out by the person who put them there. Because the pool stays in place, holders can always sell into it. It protects against the creator emptying the pool, which is the most common memecoin scam.

**Can the creator of an ArkhamPad coin remove liquidity?**
No. The pool position of every ArkhamPad coin is held by the launcher contract and cannot be withdrawn by anyone, including the creator and ArkhamPad. The lock has no end date, so a liquidity rug pull is not possible on ArkhamPad coins.

**Does locked liquidity mean a token is safe?**
No. It removes the risk of the pool being withdrawn, but the price can still fall sharply if holders sell or interest fades. Check holder concentration, trading activity and the contract address, and treat every memecoin as high risk, even one with a permanent lock.

**What is the difference between locked and burned liquidity?**
Burned liquidity is sent to an address nobody controls, so it is gone for good, along with any fees it earns. Locked liquidity is held by a contract that prevents withdrawal, either until a date or forever. A permanent contract lock, like ArkhamPad's, keeps the pool in place while still collecting trading fees.

**How do I know if a token on Elysium has locked liquidity?**
On ArkhamPad's Discover page, coins launched on ArkhamPad show an LP locked label. Tokens launched elsewhere do not carry that label, so you need to check their own terms. The token page also shows the pool type, creator and contract address, so you can confirm you are looking at the right coin before you buy.


# Memecoin Launch Checklist: Your First 24 Hours
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/memecoin-launch-checklist/

A good memecoin launch is mostly preparation: have the name, ticker, image, description, links and a little HYPE ready before you open the create form. After launch, share the token page and contract address right away, stay active in your community for the first hours, and avoid price promises. Launching on ArkhamPad takes about 30 seconds, with liquidity locked and 30% of trading fees going to the creator.

## Before launch: prepare the basics

Most failed launches fail before the coin exists. Prepare these first:

- **Name and ticker.** Short, easy to spell and easy to search. Check Discover for existing coins with the same name so yours is not mistaken for a copy.
- **Image.** Square, clear at small sizes, recognisable in a list of hundreds of tokens.
- **One-sentence idea.** What is the coin about? If you cannot say it in one line, buyers will not repeat it.
- **Description and links.** An X account and a community chat set up before launch, so the links work on day one.
- **A launch post.** Written in advance, with a space for the contract address.

None of this guarantees interest. It just removes the reasons people skip a coin.

## Before launch: fund your wallet

You need HYPE on Elysium to pay the network fee, and more if you plan a first buy. If you are starting from USDC on Base, you can deposit it on the [Bridge page](https://arkhampad.com/bridge/) and it arrives as HYPE on Elysium. The steps are in [buy Elysium tokens with USDC](https://arkhampad.com/learn/buy-elysium-tokens-with-usdc/).

Decide your first buy amount in advance, not in the moment. A large first buy means you hold a large share of supply, and traders read that as risk. Keep a small amount of HYPE aside for gas after launch, because every transaction on Elysium pays its network fee in HYPE.

## Launch: the 30-second part

On ArkhamPad the launch itself is quick:

1. Open [Create](https://arkhampad.com/create/).
2. Enter name, ticker, image, description and links.
3. Set your optional first buy.
4. Confirm the transaction.

Your coin goes live with 1,000,000,000 tokens in a Uniswap v3 style pool against HYPE, a starting market cap of 60 HYPE, and liquidity locked forever. The full walkthrough is in [how to create a token on Elysium](https://arkhampad.com/learn/create-a-token-on-elysium/).

Before confirming, check spelling one more time. A typo in the ticker is permanent.

## The first hour: what to do right after launch

The first hour sets the tone. A practical order:

1. Open your token page and copy the contract address.
2. Post your launch message on X with the token page link and the contract address. You can share to X directly from the token page.
3. Pin the contract address in your community chat.
4. Watch the live trades list and answer questions quickly.
5. Do not panic at early sells. Some buyers take quick profits. That is normal.

Posting the contract address early matters more than it seems. Copies of new coins can appear quickly, and buyers who cannot find the official address may buy the wrong one.

## Hours 2 to 24: keep the coin active

After the first rush, attention fades fast. What helps in the rest of the day:

- **Post updates, not promises.** Share milestones like new holders, community posts and memes. Never promise price targets or profits.
- **Read the chart with your community.** If people ask what a big candle means, explain it plainly. Our guide to [reading a memecoin chart](https://arkhampad.com/learn/how-to-read-a-memecoin-chart/) is a good link to share.
- **Watch holder concentration.** If a few wallets hold a large share, say so openly rather than hiding it. Traders check [top-10 holders](https://arkhampad.com/learn/token-holders-top-10/) anyway.
- **Stay reachable.** A creator who disappears in the first day is the fastest way to lose a community.

## How creator fees fit into your plan

On ArkhamPad, creators get 30% of the 1% pool fee, which is about 0.3% of trading volume. As a hypothetical example, $100,000 of volume creates $1,000 in pool fees and $300 for the creator. Fees come from activity, so a coin that keeps trading keeps paying, even if you never sell a token.

That changes the goal of the first 24 hours. The aim is not one big spike. It is a coin people want to keep trading and talking about. More on the math in [creator fees explained](https://arkhampad.com/learn/earn-creator-fees/).

## Common memecoin launch mistakes

Avoid these:

- Launching without working links, then adding them hours later.
- Spending most of your budget on the first buy and having nothing left for gas.
- Selling a large first buy in the first hour. Everyone sees it in live trades.
- Copying another coin's name or image. It confuses buyers and damages trust.
- Promising returns or listings you cannot deliver.
- Launching at a time when you cannot be online for the next few hours.

If you are planning around the chain itself, check [what traders should know about the Elysium mainnet launch](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-mainnet-launch/).

## A realistic view

Most memecoins do not take off, however good the preparation. That is the nature of the market. Treat a launch as an experiment, spend only what you can afford to lose, and judge success by whether a community forms, not by one day of price action.

## FAQ

**What should I prepare before launching a memecoin?**
Have the name, ticker, square image, a one-line idea, a short description and working links ready. Set up your X account and community chat first. Fund your wallet with HYPE for gas and any first buy, and write your launch post in advance with a space for the contract address.

**What should I do right after launching my token?**
Copy the contract address from the token page, post it on X with the token link, and pin it in your community chat. Then stay online, answer questions and watch the live trades list. Posting the official address early helps buyers avoid copycat coins.

**How much should my first buy be?**
There is no right number. Spend only what you can afford to lose, and remember that a large first buy gives you a large share of supply, which many traders treat as a warning sign. Some creators skip the first buy entirely and rely on creator fees instead.

**How do I get holders for a new memecoin?**
There is no shortcut. Clear branding, working links, an active creator and regular updates help people find the coin and stay. Sharing the token page and contract address widely, and replying to people who ask questions, does more than any single post.

**Can my memecoin launch fail even if I do everything right?**
Yes. Most memecoins never get much trading, regardless of preparation. A checklist removes avoidable mistakes, but it cannot create demand or interest. Treat a launch as a risky experiment, judge it by whether a community forms, and never spend money you cannot afford to lose.


# How to Spot a Rug Pull on Elysium: 9 Red Flags
URL: https://arkhampad.com/learn/spot-a-rug-pull/

A rug pull is when the people behind a token take buyers' money and leave the token worthless, usually by removing liquidity or dumping a large hidden supply. To spot one, check whether liquidity is locked, how much the top 10 holders own, whether you can actually sell, and whether the contract address is the official one. On ArkhamPad, coins launched there show an LP locked label, so a liquidity rug pull is not possible on them.

## What is a rug pull in crypto?

A rug pull is a scam where a token's creators or insiders pull value out of a project and leave buyers holding something they cannot sell for much. There are two broad types:

- **Hard rug:** the creator removes the liquidity pool, or uses hidden contract powers, so the token becomes unsellable or worthless in one move.
- **Soft rug:** insiders quietly hold a large share of supply, build hype, and sell into buyers over hours or days until the price collapses.

Elysium is a normal EVM chain, the same as other networks in that respect. See [Elysium vs HyperEVM](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-vs-hyperevm/) for how the two chains differ. Any open chain where anyone can launch a token also has scams. The checks below work on any token you see on Discover.

## Red flags 1 to 3: liquidity and ownership

**1. Liquidity is not locked.** If one wallet can withdraw the pool, it can empty it. This is the most direct rug. On ArkhamPad, coins launched there show an LP locked label on Discover, because the pool position is held by the launcher contract and cannot be withdrawn by anyone. Tokens from other launchpads may follow different rules. Learn more in [locked liquidity explained](https://arkhampad.com/learn/locked-liquidity-explained/).

**2. A few wallets hold most of the supply.** If the top 10 holders own a large share, they can sell into you. Open the holders list on the token page and check the top-10 share shown on Discover. Remember that the pool itself often appears as a holder. Our guide to [top-10 holder concentration](https://arkhampad.com/learn/token-holders-top-10/) explains how to read it.

**3. The creator holds a big chunk.** Check the creator address on the token page and look for it in the holders list. A creator with a large bag and no visible community is a classic soft rug setup.

## Red flags 4 to 6: the contract and selling

**4. You may not be able to sell.** Some tokens charge their own transfer tax, or block sells entirely. On ArkhamPad, tokens that charge a transfer tax may not be sellable through the router. Before buying a large amount, look at the live trades list for successful sells by other wallets. A chart with only buys is a warning sign.

**5. It is a copy.** Scammers launch tokens with the same name and image as a coin that is getting attention. Always check the contract address against the one the real project posted. You can search Discover by address, not just by name.

**6. The pool is thin.** If a small buy moves the price a lot, liquidity is low and anyone selling will crash it. The quote and minimum received before you trade tell you a lot. Learn how in [slippage explained](https://arkhampad.com/learn/slippage-explained/).

## Red flags 7 to 9: behaviour and promises

**7. Volume comes from a handful of wallets.** Look at the live trades list. If the same few addresses trade back and forth, the activity may be staged to look popular. Buys and sells counts on Discover help here too.

**8. The chart only goes one way, then suddenly not.** A perfect straight climb with no sells, followed by one giant red candle, is often an insider exit. Our guide to [reading a memecoin chart](https://arkhampad.com/learn/how-to-read-a-memecoin-chart/) shows how to read candles and volume together.

**9. Promises and pressure.** Guaranteed returns, "last chance to buy", fake partnerships, or claims of listings that cannot be checked. Real projects do not need to rush you. Anyone promising profit on a memecoin is either mistaken or lying.

## A two-minute safety routine before you buy

1. Find the token on Discover and confirm the contract address.
2. Check for the LP locked label, or the pool type on the token page.
3. Check the top-10 holder share and the creator's holdings.
4. Scroll the live trades list for real sells from different wallets.
5. Look at the age of the token and its chart history.
6. Read the quote. If a small trade has a big price impact, size down.
7. Buy a small amount first if you are unsure, and confirm you can sell.

None of this makes a memecoin safe. It removes the most obvious traps.

## What ArkhamPad coins rule out, and what they do not

Coins launched on ArkhamPad follow fixed rules: 1,000,000,000 tokens, all placed in the pool at launch, no team allocation, no presale, and liquidity locked forever. That rules out a liquidity rug pull and hidden insider allocations at launch.

It does not rule out a soft rug. The creator can make a first buy, and early buyers can accumulate a large share and sell later. Price can fall fast for many reasons. Check holders and trades on every coin, including ArkhamPad coins. For a broader view of the market, read the [Elysium memecoins guide](https://arkhampad.com/learn/elysium-memecoins-guide/).

## If you think you have been rugged

Act calmly. Check whether you can still sell part of your position, and use a higher slippage setting only if you understand the risk of a worse price. Do not follow links from strangers offering to recover funds. Those offers are almost always a second scam. Share the contract address with your community so others can avoid it.

## FAQ

**What is a rug pull in crypto?**
A rug pull is a scam where a token's creators or insiders take buyers' money and leave the token worthless. It usually happens by removing the liquidity pool, blocking sells, or dumping a large hidden supply. It is one of the most common risks with new memecoins.

**Can ArkhamPad coins be rug pulled?**
A liquidity rug pull is not possible on ArkhamPad coins, because the pool position is held by the launcher contract and cannot be withdrawn by anyone. There is also no team allocation or presale. The price can still drop sharply if holders sell, so a soft rug remains possible.

**Why can't I sell a token I bought?**
The token may charge its own transfer tax or restrict sells. On ArkhamPad, tokens with a transfer tax may not be sellable through the router. It can also be a slippage issue in a fast-moving or thin market. Check the live trades list for other wallets selling successfully before buying.

**How do I check if a token is a copy?**
Compare the contract address with the one posted by the real project on its official channels. Names, tickers and images can be copied, but the contract address cannot. On ArkhamPad you can search Discover by address to find the exact token.

**What is the difference between a soft rug and a hard rug?**
A hard rug is a single move that makes a token unsellable or worthless, like removing liquidity. A soft rug is slower: insiders holding a large share sell into buyers over time until the price collapses. Locked liquidity prevents hard rugs of the first kind but not soft rugs.
